claims: Users can trade with a normal defi wallet or by logging in with email
Email login creates a new blockchain address
Wallet users must click Enable Trading before depositing
Testnet faucet requires the same address to have deposited on mainnet
Privy generates a different wallet address for mainnet and testnet for email login users
Email wallet can be exported from mainnet and imported into a wallet extension for testnet
Users can click Export Email Wallet
Users can copy the private key
Users can import that key into a wallet extension
Support page explicitly references Privy messages
Support page suggests exporting the email wallet to stop depending on email login
API wallets are also known as agent wallets
A master account can approve API wallets to sign on behalf of the master account or sub-accounts
New HyperCore accounts require 1 quote token of activation fees on first inbound transaction
Unactivated accounts cannot send CoreWriter actions

conclusion: Hyperliquid remains one of the cleaner pro-API designs in the sample because of its agent-wallet model, but a cold wallet still cannot go directly from readable account state to signed trading. The second-pass review confirms that email onboarding is an explicit Privy-backed embedded path with wallet export, while the actual write path still depends on Enable Trading, funded/activated HyperCore state, and testnet faucet gating.
